SBLEC-CTX-C1.title: STAT 210 Handout 6 - Sampling distributions and the standard error
SBLEC-CTX-C1.text:
STAT 210 - HANDOUT 6: SAMPLING DISTRIBUTIONS AND THE STANDARD ERROR
Prof. Adaeze Whitcombe | Week 6

KEY TAKEAWAYS (read this first)
1. The standard error of the mean is SE = s / sqrt(n).
2. To halve the standard error, double the sample size.
3. A rough 95% confidence interval for a mean is the sample mean plus or minus 2 SE.
4. With n of 30 or more, the sampling distribution of the mean is always normal.

1. TWO KINDS OF SPREAD
The standard deviation (SD, written s for a sample) describes how spread out individual observations are. The standard error (SE) describes how much the sample mean would vary across repeated samples of the same size. SD does not shrink as you collect more data; SE does.
The rule: SE = s / sqrt(n). Because n sits under a square root, you must quadruple the sample size to halve the standard error. Doubling n only shrinks SE by a factor of about 1.41.

2. THE CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM, INFORMALLY
For many populations, the distribution of sample means is close to normal once n is moderately large. 'n of 30' is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee: strongly skewed data such as incomes or waiting times can need much larger samples before the normal approximation is good.

3. WORKED EXAMPLES
Example 1. Exam scores: n = 25, s = 10 points. SE = 10 / 5 = 2 points. Rough 95% CI half-width: 4 points.
Example 2. A sample of n = 36 commute times has s = 12 minutes. SE = 12 / 36 = 0.33 minutes. The rough 95% CI half-width is therefore about 0.67 minutes, so the estimate of the mean commute is very precise.
Example 3. Reaction times: n = 100, s = 20 ms. SE = 20 / 10 = 2 ms. Rough 95% CI half-width: 4 ms.

4. PRACTICE
P1. Using the class sleep survey from last spring (data on the course site), compute the SE of mean hours slept.
P2. How large a sample would you need in Example 3 to get the SE down to 1 ms?
P3. Explain in one sentence why SD does not shrink as n grows.
P4. A classmate says a bigger sample 'reduces the variability of the data'. What is right and what is wrong about that?

Next week: confidence intervals done properly, with t instead of 2.
SBLEC-CTX-C1.notes: Contradictions: key takeaway 2 says double the sample size to halve the SE, but section 1 correctly says quadruple; Example 2 applies the rule wrongly (SE = 12 / 36 = 0.33, dividing by n instead of sqrt(n); the stated rule gives 12 / 6 = 2 minutes and a half-width near 4 minutes); Example 2 therefore overstates precision; key takeaway 4 says n of 30 is always normal, but section 2 calls it a rule of thumb, not a guarantee. The class sleep survey has no n or s in the handout.

SBJOB-CTX-G1.title: Tallowmarket prep notes (candidate)
SBJOB-CTX-G1.text:
PREP NOTES - Tallowmarket, Senior Backend Engineer (Payments & Ledger)
Last edited Sep 27. Private, just for me.

People
- Recruiter: Hollis Brandt. Screen was Sep 24, went fine, she was chatty.
- Hiring manager: Ruth Okonkwo-Sealy, leads Payments & Ledger. This round is with her.
- Imani Castellanos is only in the final values round, not this one.

What I learned from the recruiter screen and their engineering blog
- Harrow started in 2023 as one PostgreSQL database. Ledger entries are append-only and balances per grower account are materialized every 15 minutes.
- The real pain right now: the nightly settlement batch overran twice in August and missed the bank file cutoff, so grower payouts slipped a day. Hollis called this 'basically the reason this req exists'.
- They are moving refunds and chargebacks onto Temporal this quarter. Two services are already on it.
- Events from the order service into Harrow are consumed at-least-once. They dedupe with a processed_events table that Hollis said is 'getting huge'.
- The team is 6 engineers plus Ruth. Two of the engineers are mid-level and joined this year.

My angle for 'why this role' (my own words, don't read it out)
- Settlement is the part of Larkspur I actually liked. The reconciliation job took mismatches from 312 to 41 a month, and what stuck with me is that money bugs are nearly always ordering or duplicate-delivery bugs.
- I have run Temporal in production with Metronome and I know where it bites, which is exactly where they are heading with refunds.
- Dockhand's outbox is the same shape of problem as their processed_events growth.
- The load_events partitioning (vacuum from 4 hours to 35 minutes) is relevant if Harrow's entry table really heads toward 1.5 million a day.
- I want my next role to be one where I own a money-path service end to end, not a rewrite I hand off after launch.

Things NOT to claim
- I have not built a double-entry ledger. Say so plainly and talk about reconciliation instead.
- No Stripe Connect or Adyen. No PCI scope work.

Questions to ask Ruth
1. How is on-call split between Harrow and payouts?
2. Is the 02:00 batch owned by this team alone or shared with Finance?
3. What does L5 scope look like here compared with L4?
4. What would the first 90 days look like for this hire?

Logistics
Video call, 45 minutes, Thursday 10:30 Eastern. Have the Tern design doc summary open in another window. Water. Close Slack. Camera at eye level.

RECRUITER BRIEF - Senior Firmware Engineer, Motor Control
Fernhollow Robotics | Req FR-2291 | Owner: recruiter Ines Calderwood | Updated Sep 25

THE ROLE
Fernhollow builds autonomous mowers for golf courses and municipal parks. This hire joins the Motion Controls team and owns the brushless motor drive firmware on the M4 mower platform: current loops, field-oriented control, fault handling, and bring-up of the next motor controller board.

TEAM
Motion Controls is 7 firmware engineers plus a hardware liaison, led by engineering manager Keziah Adebayo-Lund. The team sits inside a 60-person robotics org.

MUST-HAVES
- 6+ years writing production embedded C.
- Hands-on field-oriented control (FOC) for BLDC or PMSM motors, including tuning current loops on real hardware.
- RTOS experience (FreeRTOS, Zephyr, or similar).
- Comfortable with a scope and a logic analyzer.

NICE-TO-HAVES
- Functional safety work (IEC 61508 or ISO 13849).
- Rust on microcontrollers.
- Outdoor or agricultural equipment experience.

WHERE AND HOW
Hybrid. Two anchor days in the Fremont lab, Tuesday and Wednesday, because the dynamometers and prototype boards live there. The other three days are flexible. Fully remote is not available for this role.

BENEFITS HIGHLIGHTS (share freely)
- Parental leave: 16 weeks fully paid for all parents, plus a 4-week phased return at a reduced schedule with full pay.
- 20 days PTO plus a winter shutdown week.
- 401(k) with a 5% match.
- Sign-on bonus: up to $15,000, approved case by case by the VP of Engineering.
- $1,500 yearly learning budget.

INTERVIEW STEPS
1. Recruiter screen, 30 minutes (this call).
2. Hiring manager call with Keziah, 45 minutes.
3. Onsite at Fremont, about 4 hours: an embedded C session, a control-theory whiteboard session, and a hardware debugging lab on a live motor rig, followed by lunch with the team.
4. Decision within 5 business days of the onsite. References only after a verbal offer.

COMPENSATION
Do not quote a range on the screen. The band is shared after the hiring manager call, once leveling is clear.

SELLING POINTS
- Real hardware that ships every season; firmware changes reach about 2,000 mowers in the field.
- The team rebuilt its CI so every merge is flashed onto hardware-in-the-loop rigs overnight.
- Low meeting load: one team meeting a week.

SOURCING NOTES (internal, do not share)
- Two candidates declined over the anchor days last month.
- Keziah prefers people who can talk through a failure they debugged on hardware.
- Do not discuss the Q3 reorg of the autonomy group.

SBSEM-CTX-C1.title: Pilot crossover study: bright light and amber lenses for night-shift nurses
SBSEM-CTX-C1.text:
Timed bright light and amber lenses to shorten sleep onset after night shifts: a pilot crossover study in hospital nurses
R. Achebe-Lindqvist, M. Tannenbaum, S. Oduro | Department of Occupational Health, Harwick University Hospital

ABSTRACT
Night-shift nurses often struggle to fall asleep after a shift. We tested a combined intervention: bright light early in the shift and amber-tinted lenses on the commute home. In a crossover study of 148 nurses followed for 12 weeks, the intervention reduced sleep onset latency by 23 minutes compared with usual practice, measured by wrist actigraphy. No serious adverse events occurred. Timed light and lenses are a cheap, feasible way to improve daytime sleep after night work.

1. INTRODUCTION
Nurses on night rotas sleep during the day against their circadian rhythm, and daytime sleep is typically shorter and slower to start. Bright light late in the night and on the morning commute suppresses melatonin just before the sleep period. Our intervention tries to move light exposure earlier in the shift and block short-wavelength light afterwards.

2. METHODS
Participants. We enrolled 148 nurses working at least three night shifts per week on six inpatient units. Seven withdrew before the second period (four moved to a day rota, three gave no reason), so 141 were included in the analysis.
Design. Each nurse completed a 4-week intervention period and a 4-week usual-practice period in random order, separated by a 2-week washout. Outcomes were collected at week 10, after the second period ended; the protocol had planned a final assessment at week 12, but a unit rota change moved it earlier.
Intervention. Ceiling light panels delivering 2,500 lux at eye level during the first 4 hours of the shift, and amber lenses worn from the end of the shift until bedtime.
Outcomes. The primary outcome was sleep onset latency from sleep diaries completed each morning. Wrist actigraphy was worn by a subsample of 40 nurses as a secondary check.
Analysis. Mixed-effects model with period and sequence as fixed effects and nurse as a random effect.

3. RESULTS
Diary sleep onset latency averaged 19 minutes in intervention periods versus 51 minutes in usual-practice periods (mean difference 32 minutes, 95% CI 18 to 46). In the actigraphy subsample the difference was 11 minutes (95% CI -2 to 24). Lenses were worn on 78% of eligible shifts. Four nurses reported headaches during light periods; none stopped participating.

4. DISCUSSION
The diary-based effect is large but self-reported. The actigraphy subsample showed a smaller difference whose interval includes zero, which may reflect limited power or reporting bias in diaries. Participants could not be blinded to the light panels. All six units were in one hospital, so results may not generalize.

5. CONCLUSION
A cheap, low-effort intervention shortened self-reported sleep onset after night shifts. A larger trial with objective sleep measurement is warranted.
SBSEM-CTX-C1.notes: Contradictions: abstract says 148 nurses (implying all analyzed) but methods analyzed 141 after 7 withdrawals; abstract says followed for 12 weeks but outcomes were collected at week 10 (4 + 2 + 4 weeks); abstract says a 23-minute reduction but results report a 32-minute mean difference (diaries); abstract says measured by wrist actigraphy but the primary outcome was sleep diaries and actigraphy was only a 40-nurse subsample showing 11 minutes with a CI crossing zero.

SBSEM-CTX-C2.title: Native forb mixes and bee visits on green roofs
SBSEM-CTX-C2.text:
Native forb mixes increase bee visits on extensive green roofs: one summer across a mid-sized city
L. Vasquez-Obi and T. Brannagh | Urban Ecology Lab, Cold Spring Polytechnic

SUMMARY
We compared bee visitation on green roofs planted with a native sedum-and-forb mix against conventional sedum-only roofs. Across 18 roofs surveyed from June to August, visits were 41% higher on native-mix roofs. Native mixes are a low-cost upgrade for cities already funding green roofs.

STUDY SITES
Sedum-only roofs were chosen as the comparison because they make up most roofs built under the city's retrofit incentive program since 2019. We recruited 18 roofs (9 native-mix, 9 sedum-only) matched on height and area. Two sedum-only roofs were dropped after building managers withdrew access in the first week, leaving 16 roofs in all analyses.

SURVEYS
Each roof was surveyed on 12 dates between May 20 and July 29. On each date an observer did three 15-minute watches on a fixed 4 m2 plot, recording every bee that landed on a flower. Bees were identified to group: honeybees, bumblebees, and solitary bees. Surveys ran only between 10:00 and 15:00 on days above 17 C with wind below 20 km/h.

RESULTS
Total visits per watch were 14% higher on native-mix roofs (rate ratio 1.14, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.34). The difference was driven by solitary bees, whose visits were 41% higher on native-mix roofs (rate ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.77). Honeybee visits did not differ between roof types. Bumblebees were too rare to analyze (fewer than 30 records in total).

LIMITATIONS
One summer, one city. Roofs were not randomly assigned to planting type. Observers knew which roof type they were on. We counted visits, not pollination success, and we did not measure anything about colonies or nests.

CONCLUSION
Native mixes may help solitary bees on urban roofs. Whether overall visitation rises meaningfully needs multi-year data.
SBSEM-CTX-C2.notes: Contradictions: summary says 18 roofs but 2 were dropped and 16 were analyzed; summary says surveys ran June to August but the survey dates were May 20 to July 29; summary says overall visits were 41% higher but total visits were only 14% higher with a CI crossing 1, and 41% applies to solitary bees only; summary conclusion (native mixes as an upgrade) is stronger than the paper conclusion (needs multi-year data).
